The Hillsborough disaster was a human crush at Hillsborough football stadium in Sheffield, England, UK, on 15 April 1989, during the 1988–89 FA Cup semi-final game between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest. With 96 fatalities and 766 injured it is the worst disaster in British sporting history, and remains one of the worst recorded football disasters worldwide.

In the minutes before the match's kick-off, the central, standing only pens were already filled with supporters when, in an attempt to ease overcrowding outside the entrance turnstiles, the police ordered gates to be opened, leading to an influx of even more supporters to the already overcrowded central pens. As fans tried to escape, the police at first attempted to stop fans from spilling out of the pens, some believing this to be a pitch invasion. Those still trapped in the pens were packed so tightly that many victims died of compressive asphyxia while standing. Meanwhile, on the pitch, police and members of the St John Ambulance service were overwhelmed. Many uninjured fans assisted the injured; several attempted CPR and others tore down advertising hoardings to use as stretchers A total of 44 ambulances arrived, but police prevented all but one from entering the stadium. Only 14 of the 96 fatally injured people arrived at a hospital.

After the disaster, Lord Justice Taylor was appointed to conduct an inquiry into the events. Taylor noted that "an all some 65 police officers gave oral evidence at the Inquiry. Sadly I must report that for the most part the quality of their evidence was in inverse proportion to their rank." The Report concluded that "policing on 15 April broke down" and "although there were other causes, the main reason for the disaster was the failure of police control." The Taylor Report had a deep impact on safety standards for stadiums in the UK. Perimeter and lateral fencing was removed and many top stadiums were converted to all-seated.
